brief: A utensil holder with two bins that is waterproof and dishwasher safe.

requirements.evidence: Two hex bases (piece:0,0,0;full and piece:0,-1,0;full), capped on their open faces and bolted together (jointBolt:0#0,-1#5). A spoon and a fork stand upright in the bins. The checks passed with no overlapping parts.
Two full-depth bins: bin:0,0,0~hex-bin-full and bin:0,-1,0~hex-bin-full. Each sits in its own cell.

The configurator only checks whether parts fit. It can't check whether anything is watertight, so I can't promise this. The bins have no drain holes, but whether they hold water depends on the material and how they're printed.
The configurator knows nothing about heat or how well a material holds up in a dishwasher. Whether the parts survive one depends on the material you print them in, so I can't claim it.

finish.summary: I built the utensil holder with two bins, but I can't promise it's waterproof or dishwasher safe. The holder is two full hex bases bolted together, each with a full-depth bin, so there are 14 printed parts in all. I chose bins without drain holes. The configurator's checks passed and found no parts overlapping. To show what it's for, a spoon stands in one bin and a fork in the other.

lines.label: M6 x 25 socket head screw, ISO 4762

notes: Tighten every M6 to 2 N.m: HAND TOOLS ONLY, never a cordless driver. These bolts clamp printed PETG, not metal: at the bolt's own 10.4 N.m rating the head crushes the plastic under it and the joint fails silently, looking tight while holding nothing. Snug, then a nudge. Re-check the bolts after the first few weeks: PETG relaxes under load and the clamp will have eased.
